Every token the subagent processes is spent, not only the summary.

Run every task at low effort and accept the lower solve rate
Run every task at high effort but truncate outputs to save tokens
Ask the model at low effort to rate its own confidence and re-run only low-confidence tasks, skipping the tests

Gives up quality the cascade would recover.
Truncation breaks fixes and does not target spend at hard cases.
Self-rated confidence is not a reliable failure checker when tests are available.

Switch every subagent to the largest model to reduce the number of turns
Remove the orchestrator and answer every question with a single call without tools
Instruct the lead to scale effort to query complexity: handle simple fact-finding with one agent and a few tool calls, and fan out only for broad questions

questions.stem: A software vendor wants to add an agent to its backend service that reuses Claude Code's agent loop, built-in tools, permissions and hooks, running inside its own process. Which option fits best?

Use the Agent SDK to embed the agent loop in the service
Let the vendor's customers sign in with their claude.ai accounts so the service uses their plan limits
Use the Client SDK and re-implement the loop, tools and permission system from scratch

Possible, but it rebuilds what the requirement says to reuse.

questions.stem: Which workloads best justify the token cost of an orchestrator–subagent design? (Select two.)
options: Breadth-first research across many independent sources that can be explored in parallel
A refactor in one codebase where each change depends on earlier edits
Investigations whose source material exceeds what fits in one context window
High-volume, low-value FAQ replies where unit cost dominates
questions.explanation: Anthropic positions multi-agent systems for breadth-first, parallelisable work that exceeds a single context window. Shared-context work such as most coding is a poor fit, and low-value volume cannot absorb a roughly 15× token multiplier.
rationales: Tightly coupled, shared-context work is a poor fit.
Correct — separate contexts let the system cover more than one window.
The token multiplier destroys the unit economics.

questions.stem: A team attached an advisor (a stronger model the executor can consult) to every request in a high-volume classification pipeline. Cost rose noticeably but accuracy did not change, and logs show the executor almost never consults the advisor. What is the best interpretation?
options: The advisor needs a larger model to have an effect
The executor should be forced to consult the advisor on every request
Accuracy will improve once the cache warms up, so leave it in place
The advisor adds prompt overhead to every request even when unused and only helps when consulted, so remove it here or reserve it for paths where escalation adds value
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance notes the advisor adds prompt tokens on every request even when unused and can help only when the executor consults it. With near-zero consultation and no accuracy gain, it is pure overhead in this pipeline.
rationales: The advisor's size is irrelevant if it is never consulted.
Forcing consultation turns every request into a frontier-model call and defeats the pattern.
Caching does not create value from an unused advisor.

sources.title: Optimizing for cost and intelligence — Claude API docs

questions.stem: An internal coding agent often edits the wrong file because it passes relative paths after the working directory changes. Which change most reliably removes this failure class?
options: Add a bold warning about relative paths to the system prompt
Switch to a larger model that tracks the working directory better
Add an automatic retry when an edit lands in the wrong file
Change the file tools to require absolute paths and reject relative ones
questions.explanation: Anthropic's agent guidance treats the agent-computer interface as a design surface and recommends poka-yoke tools. Requiring absolute paths removed exactly this class of error in its own agent work, whereas prompts and bigger models only reduce the odds.
rationales: Prompt warnings are soft and still allow the mistake.
A bigger model may err less but does not eliminate the failure class.
Retrying after a wrong edit treats the symptom and may compound damage.
Correct — make the mistake impossible at the interface.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: A sponsor's business case for an agentic dispute-handling assistant multiplies the median token cost per case by monthly volume. Pilot logs show a minority of complex cases use many times the median tokens. What should the architect do?
options: Model cost from the full distribution, including the long tail, and set per-case limits or escalation for outliers
Keep the median-based estimate because outliers are rare
Drop the complex cases from the pilot so the median holds
Use the average cost of the simplest 50% of cases to be conservative
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to price the tail of the workload, not the median, because a few expensive tasks can dominate total spend. Budgets and hard limits enforced in code keep outliers bounded.
rationales: Rare but expensive cases can dominate the bill.
Hides real demand and invalidates the pilot.

sources.title: Optimizing for cost and intelligence — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A real-time intent classifier must respond in under 300 ms at very high volume. Which model choice is most appropriate to evaluate first?
options: Whichever model has the largest context window
The most capable tier at its maximum effort setting
A mid-tier model with a 20-example few-shot prompt at its highest effort setting
The fastest, lowest-cost tier at a low effort setting, validated against an intent eval set
questions.explanation: High-volume, latency-critical classification is the sweet spot for the fastest tier at low effort; Haiku-class models can even disable thinking. Confirm quality with an eval set before considering larger models or more effort.
rationales: Context size isn't the constraint for short classification inputs.
The top tier at maximum effort is overkill on cost and latency for intent classification.
High effort and a long prompt add latency and cost a simple task doesn't need.
Correct. Smallest viable tier, low effort, eval-gated.

Send all traffic to the most capable model
Send all traffic to the cheapest model
Route with a lightweight classifier: simple questions to a cheaper tier, complex ones to a stronger tier, with evals on the router

sources.title: Optimizing for cost and intelligence — Claude API docs

Write the rules in capital letters
Move all rules into the user message
Add 60 more conditionals for the new failures
questions.explanation: Principles with reasons generalise to unseen cases; long conditional lists are brittle and dilute attention.
rationales: Persistent rules belong in the system prompt.

questions.stem: A chatbot uses a 20k-token system prompt and tool definitions that are identical across requests, but cache hit rates are near zero. The prompt begins with 'Current time: {timestamp}'. What is the fix?
options: Increase the cache TTL
Move the timestamp after the cache breakpoint (e.g., into the latest user turn) so the stable prefix is identical
Disable caching since it doesn't work for chatbots
Shorten the system prompt to below the minimum cacheable length
questions.explanation: Any change in the prefix invalidates the cache. Volatile values must come after the cached, stable content.
rationales: TTL doesn't help when the prefix changes every request.
Chatbots with long stable prefixes are ideal for caching.

sources.title: Prompt caching — Claude API docs

questions.stem: For which workload does prompt caching provide the least benefit?
options: An agent reusing a large, fixed tool set across many turns
Many questions asked against the same 100-page contract
A support bot with a long, stable system prompt
One-off summarisation of unique documents, each processed once
questions.explanation: Caching pays off when the same prefix is reused within the cache lifetime. Unique one-off prompts get no reuse.
rationales: Stable tools are a prime caching target.

questions.stem: On a model where thinking is always on, where does raising the effort level most likely improve outcomes enough to justify the extra latency and output tokens? (Select two.)
options: Extracting a customer's name from an email signature
Debugging a subtle concurrency bug across several files
Classifying sentiment of short tweets at high volume
Planning a complex multi-step data migration with many constraints
questions.explanation: Higher effort means more thinking, which helps complex reasoning, planning and hard debugging. Thinking tokens are billed as output, so simple extraction and high-volume classification should stay at low effort or move to a smaller model.
rationales: Simple extraction gains little from more reasoning.
Correct. Subtle multi-file debugging benefits from deeper reasoning.
High-volume simple classification: keep effort low.
Correct. Constraint-heavy planning benefits from deeper reasoning.

sources.title: Thinking and effort — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A long-running agent degrades after hours of work: it repeats investigations and forgets earlier conclusions. Which technique addresses this most directly?
options: Compaction plus structured notes: summarise history into decisions/findings and persist notes outside the context window
Add more tools
Restart the session from scratch every hour, discarding all state
Increase the model's max output tokens
questions.explanation: Context accumulates stale tool output. Compaction and external notes preserve key state while freeing context.
rationales: More tools add more context pressure.

sources.title: Effective context engineering — Anthropic Engineering

options: Paste all 40 procedures into the system prompt
Package each as an Agent Skill with a clear description of when it applies, relying on progressive disclosure
Fine-tune a model on the procedures
Ask users to paste the relevant procedure each time
questions.explanation: Skills keep only names/descriptions in context and load full content when relevant — scalable and maintainable.
rationales: Bloats every request and dilutes attention.

sources.title: Agent Skills overview — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Which layers form a defence-in-depth guardrail design for a customer chatbot? (Select three.)
options: Output checks for PII and policy violations before display
Relying solely on a carefully worded system prompt
Input screening for jailbreak/out-of-scope attempts with a lightweight classifier
Server-side validation and least-privilege permissions in tools
questions.explanation: Guardrails are layered across input, prompt, tools, output and monitoring. A prompt alone is a soft control.
rationales: Single soft control — not defence in depth.

sources.title: Mitigate jailbreaks and injections — Claude API docs

Switch immediately; newer versions are strictly better
Run the regression eval suite on the new version, compare cost/latency, then stage the rollout

rationales: Reactive; misses benefits and leaves migration to the last minute.

Split across multiple user turns interleaved with the question
Only a summary should be included
After the question, at the very end

Remove the system prompt

Explicitly permit and describe 'I don't know' / escalation behaviour when information isn't in provided sources

questions.stem: An orchestrator agent uses a top-tier model; subagents perform narrow file searches and summarisation. Costs are high. What change is most defensible?
options: Remove subagents and stuff everything into the orchestrator context
Raise the subagents to the highest effort setting
Downshift the orchestrator to the smallest model
Evaluate a cheaper tier for the narrow subagent tasks while keeping the stronger model for orchestration
questions.explanation: Mixed-model designs keep capability where reasoning is hard (planning and synthesis) and use cheaper tiers for narrow, well-defined work. Subagents are a context-management tool, not a discount, so the cost lever is the model they run on, validated by evals.
rationales: Higher effort increases output tokens and cost.

options: Switch to the most capable tier immediately, because benchmark gains transfer to every task
Raise the effort level on the current model and re-run the eval; consider the higher tier only if the highest effort levels still fall short
Add 'CRITICAL: be more accurate' to the system prompt
Set a larger thinking budget_tokens value on the request
questions.explanation: Anthropic's model-selection guidance says tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models; the capability-first path moves up a tier only if evals at the highest effort levels still fall short. Manual budget_tokens is no longer accepted on current models.
rationales: Skips the cheaper lever and assumes public benchmarks transfer to this task.
Correct. Effort first, eval-gated, then a tier change if needed.
Aggressive wording doesn't add capability and can cause overtriggering.
Manual thinking with budget_tokens returns 400 on Opus 4.7 and later.

options: Run every task at low effort and accept the lower solve rate
Run every task at low effort, then re-run only the tasks whose tests fail at high effort
Ask the model to self-report its confidence and escalate when it says it is unsure
Randomly assign half of the tasks to high effort and half to low
questions.explanation: A low-then-high cascade spends high effort only on the hard tail. Anthropic's internal results showed a similar or better solve rate at a much lower cost per task. It works here because the test suite is a reliable failure checker.

Correct. The cheap pass handles most tasks and the tests decide what to escalate.
Self-reported confidence is a weak failure signal compared with deterministic tests.
Ignores difficulty, so it wastes high effort on easy tasks and misses hard ones.

questions.stem: An extraction service prefilled the assistant turn with '{' to force JSON. After the team upgrades to Opus 5.5, every request fails with HTTP 400. What is the right migration?
options: Force the extraction tool with tool_choice set to that specific tool
Move to structured outputs with a JSON schema in output_config.format, and handle refusal and max_tokens stops
Keep the prefill and add a beta header to re-enable it
Remove the prefill and add 'RESPOND ONLY IN JSON' in capitals

No such re-enable path is documented; prefill returns 400.
Instructions alone give no schema guarantee, and capitals tend to cause overtriggering.

Structured outputs can be combined with citations in the same request
Setting tool_choice to a specific tool is the recommended way to force a structured response on this model
Marking a tool with strict: true and leaving tool_choice on auto yields schema-conformant tool inputs

Soften the wording and explain when search is useful (for example, questions about policy or product facts) and when it is not
Remove the search tool entirely
Raise the effort level so the model thinks harder before calling tools

Search is still needed for real knowledge questions.
More thinking doesn't override an explicit instruction to always search, and it adds latency.

sources.title: Prompting best practices — Claude API docs

questions.stem: To cut latency, a developer sends thinking: {type: 'disabled'} on a quick-reply path that runs on Sonnet 5.5, and the API returns 400. What is the most appropriate design response?
options: Use manual thinking with a very small budget_tokens value instead
Tell the model in the system prompt not to think
Increase max_tokens so the thinking finishes faster
Lower the effort level on this path, or move it to a model that allows disabling thinking (such as Haiku 5.5), and confirm quality and latency with evals

rationales: Manual budget_tokens returns 400 on Opus 4.7 and later models.
Prompt text doesn't change the API's thinking behaviour.
max_tokens is a ceiling, not a speed control.

sources.title: Thinking and effort — Claude API docs

questions.stem: After raising effort to high for a planning agent, the team sees more responses that end with stop_reason max_tokens and a partial answer, and the bill for output tokens has grown. What explains both?
options: Higher effort increases input tokens through prompt caching
Thinking tokens are billed as output and count toward max_tokens, so max_tokens needs headroom for the extra reasoning
High effort disables the cache, which shortens responses
The model's context window shrinks at higher effort
questions.explanation: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens and count toward max_tokens. Higher effort means more thinking, so the same max_tokens leaves less room for the visible answer and output spend rises.
rationales: Effort affects thinking (output), not cached input.
Changing effort invalidates the messages cache but doesn't truncate responses.
The context window is fixed per model.

sources.title: Thinking and effort — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A team adds cache_control to a short, fixed system prompt of a few hundred tokens on a high-traffic Sonnet 5.5 endpoint. Usage shows cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are both 0 on every request. What is the most likely cause?
options: The 5-minute TTL expires between requests
The prompt is below the model's minimum cacheable length, so it is silently not cached
More than four breakpoints were defined
Caching only works with the Batch API
questions.explanation: Prompts below the minimum cacheable length (512 tokens on the newest models) are silently not cached, and both cache usage fields stay at 0. An expired TTL would still show cache creation tokens on the next write, and the four-breakpoint limit is not what produces silent zeros on every request.
rationales: With high traffic the TTL keeps being refreshed, and an expiry would still show writes.
The breakpoint limit is a request constraint; it does not explain silent zeros on a short, fixed prompt.
Caching works on standard requests, and its multipliers also stack with Batch.

sources.title: Prompt caching — Claude API docs

questions.stem: An agent builds its tools array per turn, adding or removing tools depending on what the user just asked. The system prompt and documents are stable, yet cache reads are rare. What is the best fix?
options: Put the tools after the messages so they don't affect the cached prefix
Switch to the 1-hour TTL
Keep a stable tool list across turns and enforce which tools may run in code or permissions, so the cached prefix stays identical
Add more cache breakpoints inside the system prompt
questions.explanation: The cache prefix order is tools → system → messages, and changing tools invalidates everything after them. Keeping tool definitions stable restores hits; access control belongs in deterministic code, not in reshaping the prompt.
rationales: The prefix order is fixed; tools always come first.
A longer TTL doesn't help when the prefix changes each turn.
Breakpoints after a changed tools block still miss.

sources.title: Prompt caching — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Analysts query the same 60k-token policy corpus through an internal tool, but requests typically arrive 15–30 minutes apart throughout the day. Which caching setup fits best?
options: The default 5-minute TTL, since it is refreshed on use
A 1-hour TTL on the corpus prefix, accepting a higher write premium in exchange for hits across the gaps
No caching, because requests aren't back to back
Send the requests through the Batch API to keep the cache warm
questions.explanation: The 5-minute cache would expire between most requests, so every call would pay a write. A 1-hour TTL costs more to write (about 2× base input vs about 1.25×), but repeated cheap reads within the hour quickly repay it.
rationales: Refresh-on-use doesn't help when gaps exceed 5 minutes.
Leaves easy savings unused on a large, reused prefix.
Batch is for asynchronous bulk jobs, not interactive analyst queries.

sources.title: Prompt caching — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Which statements about prompt caching economics and behaviour are correct? (Select two.)
options: Cache reads are billed at a small fraction of the base input price, while cache writes carry a premium
Prompt caching multipliers stack with the Batch API discount
There is no limit on how many cache breakpoints a request can define
Changing the effort setting between requests has no effect on cache hits
questions.explanation: Writes cost a premium (about 1.25× for 5 minutes, 2× for 1 hour) and reads a fraction of base input, and these multipliers stack with Batch. Requests allow at most four breakpoints, and changing effort or thinking parameters invalidates the messages cache.
rationales: False: at most 4 breakpoints are allowed.
False: changing output_config.effort invalidates cached messages.

sources.title: Prompt caching — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A platform team wants to install 150 Agent Skills for its engineers and worries this will crowd the context window on every request. What is the accurate picture of the ongoing context cost?
options: All 150 SKILL.md bodies load into every request
Only each Skill's name and description (roughly 100 tokens per Skill) is always loaded; bodies load when a Skill is triggered, and files and scripts only as needed
Nothing loads until a user types the Skill's exact name
Bundled script source code is loaded up front so Claude can decide whether to run it
questions.explanation: Skills use progressive disclosure: L1 metadata is always present at about 100 tokens per Skill, the L2 body loads when triggered, and L3 resources load only as needed. A script's code never enters context; only its output does.
rationales: Claude selects Skills from their descriptions; users needn't name them.
Script code never enters context; only its output does.

sources.title: Agent Skills overview — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A custom Skill for producing quarterly board reports rarely activates, even when users ask for a board report. Its frontmatter description reads 'Report helper.' What is the most effective fix?
options: Rewrite the description to state what the Skill does and when to use it (for example, quarterly board reports, their audience and format), within the length limit
Move all of the instructions into the name field
Add 'ALWAYS USE THIS SKILL' in capitals to the SKILL.md body
Make the SKILL.md body much longer so the Skill seems more important
questions.explanation: Claude decides whether to load a Skill from its L1 metadata alone. The description must say what the Skill does and when to use it, within 1,024 characters; the body is invisible until the Skill is triggered.
rationales: The name is limited to 64 lowercase characters, digits and hyphens and isn't meant for instructions.
The body isn't seen until after triggering, and capitals cause overtriggering.
Body length doesn't affect triggering and adds context cost once loaded.

sources.title: Agent Skills overview — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A health-tech company runs a HIPAA-enabled organization under a signed BAA. It wants to package its clinical-note summarization procedure, which handles PHI, as an Agent Skill on the API. What should the architect advise?
options: Proceed, because every API feature is covered once the BAA is signed
Proceed, but enable Zero Data Retention to make Skills eligible

Agent Skills aren't HIPAA-eligible and requests using them will be rejected in a HIPAA-enabled org, so implement the PHI path with eligible features (for example a system prompt with prompt caching) and reserve Skills for non-PHI work in a separate org
Use the Skill but redact PHI in the SKILL.md body
questions.explanation: Agent Skills (and the code execution they rely on) are not eligible for HIPAA or ZDR. HIPAA enforcement is org-level and returns 400 for non-eligible features, so PHI work must use eligible features, and the docs suggest a separate org for non-PHI workloads.
rationales: Eligibility is per feature; Skills are excluded.
The PHI would still flow through a non-eligible feature at runtime.

sources.title: Agent Skills overview — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A team built a custom 'release-notes' Skill and uploaded it through the API for its internal service. Engineers now expect to use it in Claude Code, but it doesn't appear. What is the right approach?
options: Wait for it to sync, since custom Skills propagate across surfaces automatically
Upload it to claude.ai, which publishes it to every surface
Distribute it separately for Claude Code, for example by committing it to the repository's .claude/skills/ directory
Add the API skill_id to each engineer's CLAUDE.md
questions.explanation: Custom Skills don't sync across surfaces (API, claude.ai, Claude Code). Claude Code loads Skills from ~/.claude/skills/ or a project's .claude/skills/, so committing it to the repo shares it with the team.
rationales: claude.ai uploads don't sync to other surfaces either.
CLAUDE.md is context, not a Skill installation mechanism.

sources.title: Agent Skills overview — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A Skill used through the API includes a script that pip-installs a PDF library and then downloads a currency-rate table from a public URL. It fails in every run. What is the best redesign?
options: Retry the script with a longer timeout
Bundle the needed dependencies and reference data with the Skill (or use what the container provides), and fetch live rates through a separate tool outside the container
Move the pip install command into the Skill's description
Use the pre-built pdf Skill and keep the URL download in the script
questions.explanation: The API code-execution container has no network access and no runtime package installs. Dependencies and static data must be bundled or already available, and live data must come through a tool that runs outside the container.
rationales: The failure is a missing capability, not slowness.
The network download would still fail inside the container.

sources.title: Agent Skills overview — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A vendor offers a free bundle of Agent Skills with helper scripts, some of which fetch content from external URLs. The operations team wants to install it organisation-wide today. What should the architect require?
options: Install it, since Skills are sandboxed and therefore harmless
Install it only for administrators
Treat it like third-party software: audit the instructions, scripts and bundled files, use it only if the source is trusted, and assess the prompt-injection risk of its external fetches
Rename the Skills to avoid conflicts and install them
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to use only trusted Skills and audit them like software, because they can contain executable scripts and instructions. Skills that fetch external content carry prompt-injection risk.
rationales: Sandboxing limits but doesn't remove the risk from malicious instructions or fetched content.
Narrowing the audience doesn't replace a review.

sources.title: Agent Skills overview — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Mid-way through a long session, a coding agent's context is dominated by large, old file listings and test logs it no longer needs. Its recent reasoning and decisions are still valuable. What is the lightest-touch first step?
options: Clear the stale tool results while keeping the conversation's reasoning and decisions
Start a brand-new session with no history
Switch to a model with a larger context window
Ask the model to summarise the entire session from scratch every turn
questions.explanation: Anthropic's context-engineering guidance calls tool-result clearing the lightest touch: it removes bulky, stale outputs while preserving reasoning. Compaction, structured notes and subagents are heavier options.
rationales: A larger window doesn't fix context rot and adds cost.
Repeated full summarisation is costly and can lose detail.

sources.title: Effective context engineering — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: To improve reasoning quality on a 5.x model, a team adds a required 'reasoning' string field to its structured-output schema and asks the model to explain its chain of thought there. They now see refusals and inconsistent results. What should they do instead?
options: Make the reasoning field longer and mark it required
Remove the reasoning field, rely on built-in adaptive thinking and raise effort if evals show a need, and use summarized thinking display if visibility is required
Switch to prefill with '<thinking>' to force visible reasoning
Ask for reasoning in capitals at the top of the system prompt
questions.explanation: On current models, thinking is built in and controlled by effort. Asking for reasoning in an output field or schema risks reasoning_extraction refusals, and classic visible chain of thought is a fallback only. Summarized display gives visibility without extraction.
rationales: Doubles down on the cause of the refusals.
Aggressive wording doesn't fix the extraction problem and can cause overtriggering.

sources.title: Thinking and effort — Claude API docs

questions.stem: An enterprise assistant uses a service account that can read all SharePoint sites. An intern receives an answer quoting an executive compensation memo. What is the root cause and correct fix?
options: Confused deputy; propagate the user's identity and filter retrieval by the user's ACLs before content reaches the model
Prompt injection; add 'do not reveal confidential data' to the system prompt
Chunking error; use smaller chunks
Hallucination; switch to a stronger model
questions.explanation: A privileged component served a requester without that privilege. Authorization must be enforced in code at retrieval time with the user's identity.
rationales: Prompt instructions don't enforce access control.
Chunk size is unrelated to permissions.
The content was real, not invented.

sources.title: MCP security best practices — MCP docs

questions.stem: An agent has 140 tools from 12 MCP servers and frequently selects the wrong tool. What should be tried first?
options: Switch to the most capable model
Consolidate overlapping tools, clarify descriptions and expose only task-relevant tool subsets
Add a tool that lists all other tools
Increase max tokens
questions.explanation: Tool bloat and overlapping descriptions cause selection errors, so reducing, namespacing and clarifying the tool set is the direct fix. A bigger model treats the symptom at higher cost.

sources.title: Define tools — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Users report that searches for exact part numbers like 'AX-4471-B' return irrelevant passages, though conceptual questions work well. What change is most effective?
options: Tell the model to try harder in the system prompt
Switch to a larger embedding model
Add BM25/keyword search in a hybrid retrieval setup, with reranking
Increase chunk size
questions.explanation: Exact identifiers are a lexical-matching problem that embeddings handle poorly; hybrid search fixes it. Pairing BM25 with embeddings and then reranking was among the most effective combinations in Anthropic's contextual retrieval tests.
rationales: Embeddings are still weak at exact strings.

sources.title: Contextual retrieval — Anthropic

questions.stem: Chunks such as 'Revenue grew 3% over the prior quarter' are retrieved without knowing which company or period they refer to. Which technique addresses this?
options: Reduce top-k to 1
Remove metadata from chunks
Use a larger context window
Contextual retrieval: prepend a short generated description of each chunk's document context before embedding and indexing
questions.explanation: Contextual retrieval restores meaning lost by chunking and improves both embedding and keyword retrieval. Anthropic applies the generated context to both the embeddings and the BM25 index.

sources.title: Contextual retrieval — Anthropic

questions.stem: A 30-page clinical guideline is consulted on every request and rarely changes. What is the simplest effective design?
options: Include the guideline in the prompt as a stable prefix with prompt caching
Fine-tune a model on the guideline
Build a multi-agent retrieval system
Build a vector database with hybrid search and reranking
questions.explanation: When knowledge fits comfortably in context and is reused, long context plus caching is simpler and often more accurate than RAG. Anthropic's guidance is that a knowledge base under about 200,000 tokens can go straight into the prompt.
rationales: Unnecessary complexity for a small stable corpus.

sources.title: Prompt caching — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Platform engineering wants a capability (querying the internal deployment system) available in Claude Code, a custom support agent and Claude desktop apps. What integration approach fits best?
options: Implement the tool three times, once per client
Build a single MCP server exposing the capability, governed via an allowlist and least-privilege auth
Paste API docs into each system prompt
Use agent-to-agent delegation to a vendor agent
questions.explanation: MCP's value is reuse: one server behind a standard interface can serve every MCP-capable client. Governance comes from the allowlist and least-privilege auth, not from duplicating the tool.
rationales: Model can't call an API from docs alone.
No external vendor agent is involved.

questions.stem: An MCP server receives a user's OAuth token from the client and forwards it unchanged to a downstream ticketing API. Why is this a problem?
options: It prevents caching
It increases latency

Token passthrough bypasses the server's own validation and audience checks, creating confused-deputy and accountability risks; the server should validate tokens issued for it and use its own properly scoped downstream credentials
OAuth tokens can't be sent over HTTP
questions.explanation: The MCP security guidance says servers MUST NOT accept any tokens that were not explicitly issued for them. Passing the client token through skips audience validation and blurs who is acting, which creates confused-deputy and audit risks; the server should obtain its own properly scoped downstream credentials.
rationales: Tokens are sent over HTTPS routinely.

sources.title: MCP security best practices — MCP docs

questions.stem: Which tool error response best supports agent recovery?
options: Returning the raw stack trace
Returning an empty string
Throwing an exception that terminates the agent loop
Returning a structured error such as {"error":"INVALID_DATE","message":"date must be YYYY-MM-DD","retryable":true}
questions.explanation: Structured, actionable errors let the model correct inputs or choose a different path; empties are misread and exceptions end the loop. Stack traces leak internals and give the model nothing it can act on.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: Which practices implement least privilege for a banking agent? (Select three.)
options: Separate read tools from write tools, with writes requiring confirmation
Per-user delegated credentials scoped to the customer's own accounts
Credentials held in the tool layer, never exposed to the model
A single admin token shared by all sessions to avoid auth failures
questions.explanation: Least privilege means minimal scopes, user-bound credentials, read/write separation and secrets kept from the model. A shared admin token gives every session the widest possible blast radius.

sources.title: MCP security best practices — MCP docs

questions.stem: Retrieval returns 50 candidate chunks; only 5 fit the latency/token budget. Which step improves which 5 are chosen?
options: Choosing the 5 newest documents
Reranking the candidates by relevance to the query
Random sampling
Choosing the 5 longest chunks
questions.explanation: A reranker rescores a wide candidate set so the most relevant chunks enter context. Retrieving wide and reranking narrow is the standard pattern.

sources.title: Contextual retrieval — Anthropic

questions.stem: A knowledge assistant must answer within a p95 of 4 seconds. Current pipeline: query rewrite (large model) → 3 sequential retrievals → rerank → large model at the highest effort level → verification pass. p95 is 11 s. Which changes are most appropriate? (Select two.)
options: Add another verification pass to improve accuracy
Remove the user's permission filtering to reduce latency
Use a small, fast model for query rewriting and run retrievals in parallel
Route only complex queries to high effort and the verification pass; answer simple ones at a lower effort level
questions.explanation: The targeted latency levers are cheaper models for auxiliary steps, parallel retrieval, and spending high effort and verification only where the query needs them. Authorization filtering is never traded away for latency.
rationales: Security controls aren't negotiable for latency.

sources.title: Thinking and effort — Claude API docs

questions.stem: In a multi-agent ops system, engineers can't reconstruct why a remediation was proposed. What is the most important observability addition?
options: A daily summary email
More detailed system prompts
Larger log retention
End-to-end distributed tracing with a correlation ID across orchestrator, subagents, model calls and tool calls, recording prompt/model versions and tool inputs/outputs
questions.explanation: Traces linking every step are essential for debugging and auditing multi-agent behaviour. Without linked traces, logs from separate agents cannot be put back in causal order.
rationales: Retention without linkage doesn't help reconstruct causality.

sources.title: Multi-agent research system — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: A team wants Claude Code to interact with git, the cloud provider and the package manager. Mature CLIs exist for all three. What is usually the simplest effective integration?
options: Let Claude Code use the existing CLIs, governed by permission allow/deny rules
Write a REST wrapper service around each CLI
Use agent-to-agent delegation
Build custom MCP servers for each
questions.explanation: Coding agents can use mature CLIs directly; permissions provide governance with the fewest moving parts. Wrappers or custom servers add components to build and maintain without adding capability.

sources.title: MCP in Claude Code — Claude Code docs

questions.stem: Which metadata is most important to attach to chunks in a permissioned enterprise RAG index?
options: Font and colour of the original document
Source, owner, last-modified date and access-control information
The embedding model's version only
Word count only
questions.explanation: Source and dates enable citations and freshness; ACL metadata enables permission filtering at query time. Without ACL metadata, permission filtering at query time is impossible.

sources.title: Contextual retrieval — Anthropic

questions.stem: Which signals should be logged per model call for observability at scale? (Select three.)
options: Stop reason and latency
Unredacted customer PII for easier debugging
Prompt template version and model version
Input, output and cached token counts
questions.explanation: Versions, token usage, stop reasons and latency are core telemetry. PII must be redacted or tokenised.

sources.title: API errors — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A payment tool may be retried by the agent after a timeout. What design property prevents duplicate payments?
options: Higher timeout values only
Telling the model never to retry
Logging every retry
Idempotency keys on the payment tool
questions.explanation: Idempotency ensures repeated calls with the same key have a single effect. Telling the model not to retry is a soft control and cannot make a timed-out call safe.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: Two business units each own an agent; one needs to delegate contract-review tasks to the other's agent, which runs on separate infrastructure under different governance. Which integration best fits?
options: Agent-to-agent delegation with a defined contract, authenticated identity and cross-boundary tracing
Share a single service account between both agents
Email the other team
Copy the other unit's prompts into your agent
questions.explanation: Agent-to-agent integration suits cross-ownership boundaries but requires explicit contracts, auth and observability. A shared service account would erase the ownership boundary the two units need.

sources.title: Building effective agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: A third-party MCP server from an unknown publisher offers useful tools. What is the right governance stance?
options: Install it org-wide immediately
Treat it as third-party code: vet the publisher and code, pin the version, limit scopes and add it to a central allowlist only after review
Allow each developer to decide
Ban all MCP servers
questions.explanation: MCP servers execute code and supply text the model treats as context; they need supply-chain style governance. Banning all servers is an over-correction that throws away the value.

sources.title: MCP security best practices — MCP docs
MCP in Claude Code — Claude Code docs

questions.stem: Which answer-generation practices reduce unsupported claims in RAG? (Select two.)
options: Provide an explicit 'not found in sources' response path
Remove the documents' titles to save tokens
Instruct the model to answer only from provided sources and cite the passages used
Allow answering from general knowledge when sources are thin, without saying so
questions.explanation: Grounding instructions, citations and a sanctioned 'not found' path reduce hallucination. Silently mixing in general knowledge produces claims no source supports.

sources.title: Reduce hallucinations — Claude API docs
Citations — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Which is a characteristic of MCP?
options: A vector database
A fine-tuning format
A proprietary Anthropic-only API
An open protocol for connecting AI applications to tools, resources and prompts, over local (stdio) or remote (HTTP) transports
questions.explanation: MCP is an open standard with server primitives for tools, resources and prompts. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0, and the protocol is not Anthropic-proprietary.

sources.title: MCP architecture — MCP docs

questions.stem: A chat assistant on Opus 5.5 at its default effort meets the accuracy bar with room to spare, but p95 latency misses the SLO. What should the architect try first?
options: Send `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` on every request
Add a second model to verify each answer
Set a small manual `budget_tokens` value for thinking
Lower the effort level and re-run the eval set to confirm accuracy still holds
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is that tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models, and accuracy headroom is exactly what lower effort spends. Thinking cannot be disabled on Opus 5.5 and manual `budget_tokens` returns 400 on current models.
rationales: Returns 400 on Opus 5.5; thinking cannot be disabled there.
Adds latency to a path that is already too slow.
Manual thinking budgets return 400 on Opus 4.7 and later.
Correct: lower effort, then verify with evals.

sources.title: Thinking and effort — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A nightly job fixes thousands of small config defects. Each fix can be checked automatically by a test suite. Running everything at high effort works but is expensive. Which design best cuts cost without losing solved cases?
options: Run everything at max effort on the largest model to minimise retries
Split the job across many parallel subagents at high effort
Run all items at low effort, then re-run only the items that fail the tests at high effort
Run everything at low effort and accept the failures
questions.explanation: A low-then-high cascade spends high effort only on the hard tail, and it works here because the test suite is a reliable failure checker. In Anthropic's internal benchmark the cascade solved slightly more tasks at a lower cost per task than running everything at high.
rationales: Raises cost on the easy majority.
Subagents spend their own tokens; they are not a discount.
Gives up the hard cases the job exists to fix.

sources.title: Thinking and effort — Claude API docs
Optimizing for cost and intelligence — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A team must enrich 400,000 archived documents with summaries. Nobody is waiting on the results, which are due next week. Which option best fits?
options: The Batch API, which is 50% cheaper and asynchronous
Fast mode, to finish sooner
Streaming responses for each document
A synchronous loop at the highest effort level
questions.explanation: Offline work with no latency requirement is the case Batch is built for, at half the price. Fast mode and streaming buy speed or perceived speed, which this job doesn't need.
rationales: Pays a premium for speed nobody needs.
Improves perceived latency for a waiting user; there is none.
Most expensive option with no benefit.

sources.title: API and data retention — Claude API docs

questions.stem: Finance users ask the assistant questions such as "What was total Q3 bookings by region?" The data lives in a warehouse table. The team proposes embedding table rows into the vector index. What is the better design?
options: Embed the rows with a larger embedding model
Increase top-k so more rows are retrieved
Paste the full table into every prompt
Give the agent a read-only SQL or query tool scoped to the user's permissions
questions.explanation: Retrieval should match the shape of the data: aggregations over structured data are a query problem, not a semantic-similarity problem. A scoped, read-only query tool gives exact answers and keeps least privilege.
rationales: Semantic search can't sum or group rows reliably.
More rows still don't compute an aggregate.
Wastes context and fails as the table grows.

sources.title: Define tools — Claude API docs
Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: An operations agent connects to 25 MCP servers. Tool definitions alone consume a large share of every request, and the agent confuses `list_tickets` from two different systems. Which change addresses both problems?
options: Use progressive tool discovery (tool search) and namespace tool names by service
Raise the model's context window
Add "choose tools carefully" to the system prompt in capitals
Force a specific tool with `tool_choice` on each turn
questions.explanation: Tool search loads only the tools a task needs instead of every definition, and namespacing such as `jira_list_tickets` versus `servicenow_list_tickets` removes the name collision. Aggressive capitalised instructions tend to cause overtriggering, and forced `tool_choice` returns 400 on the newest models.
rationales: More room doesn't fix ambiguity or per-request cost.
Soft wording doesn't remove the collision and can overtrigger.
Forcing a tool returns 400 on the newest models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1), and you rarely know the right tool in advance.

sources.title: Define tools — Claude API docs
Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: A CRM MCP tool returns a 40,000-token JSON payload full of UUIDs, and the agent often cites the wrong record. Which changes best fix the tool? (Select two.)
options: Add a `response_format` parameter with `concise` and `detailed` options, plus pagination and filtering
Raise `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` so the full payload always fits
Return high-signal fields and resolve UUIDs to human-readable names alongside stable IDs
Tell the model in the system prompt to ignore irrelevant fields
questions.explanation: Anthropic's tool-writing guidance recommends concise/detailed response modes, pagination and filtering, and resolving opaque UUIDs to readable names, which reduced hallucinated references. Raising the cap or asking the model to ignore noise leaves the bloat in context.
rationales: Treats the symptom and keeps the token cost.
The noisy payload still enters context.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: An MCP proxy server uses one static OAuth client ID with a third-party authorization server that supports dynamic client registration and remembers consent with a cookie. A security review flags a confused-deputy risk. Which control does the MCP security guidance require of the proxy?
options: Obtain per-client user consent in the proxy before forwarding to the third-party authorization server
Rely on the third-party consent cookie, since the user already approved once
Request a broader scope once so users are not prompted again
Log every authorization code issued
questions.explanation: The MCP guidance requires proxies to obtain per-client consent before forwarding, together with exact `redirect_uri` matching and a validated single-use `state`. The existing consent cookie is what the attacker exploits to get codes without the user's consent.
rationales: The cookie is the mechanism being abused.
Wider scopes increase blast radius and violate scope minimisation.
Logging records the attack but doesn't prevent it.

sources.title: MCP security best practices — MCP docs

questions.stem: A remote MCP server fetches URLs that come from clients during metadata discovery. A penetration test shows it can be made to request `http://169.254.169.254/` and internal admin endpoints. What is the appropriate mitigation?
options: Require HTTPS for all fetched URLs
Add a prompt telling the model not to supply internal URLs
Block private and link-local IP ranges and route outbound fetches through an egress proxy
Cache fetched responses for 24 hours
questions.explanation: This is server-side request forgery. The MCP security guidance calls for blocking private IP ranges and using an egress proxy; prompt instructions are no defence because the URL can come from an attacker.
rationales: An attacker can still target internal HTTPS hosts.
The model isn't the only source of URLs, and prompts don't enforce anything.

sources.title: MCP security best practices — MCP docs

questions.stem: An MCP server issues opaque handles for long-running searches. Any caller presenting a valid handle can read the results. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing; handles are unguessable so they are secure
Handles should be shorter to reduce token use
Possession of a handle is being treated as authentication; bind each handle to the authenticated user and check it on every request
Move to the stdio transport so handles stay local
questions.explanation: The MCP guidance calls this state-handle hijacking: because the protocol is stateless, handles must be bound to the authenticated user, and holding one is not proof of identity. Unguessability alone fails once a handle leaks through logs or shared links.
rationales: Leaked handles would expose other users' data.
Changes the transport, not the authorization flaw, and doesn't suit a remote server.

sources.title: MCP security best practices — MCP docs

questions.stem: A repository commits an `.mcp.json` file. In interactive sessions engineers are asked to approve its servers, but a CI job running `claude -p` connected to one of them without any prompt. What explains this, and how can the CI job exclude that server?
options: Headless and SDK runs load project MCP servers without a prompt; list the server in `disabledMcpjsonServers` (or run CI with `--bare`)
CI ignored `.mcp.json`; the server must have come from user scope
Project-scoped servers always override managed servers; remove the managed policy
SSE servers bypass approval; switch the server to stdio
questions.explanation: The Claude Code docs state that `-p`, SDK and cloud sessions load project servers without a prompt, and `disabledMcpjsonServers` blocks a specific one. `--bare` skips MCP entirely and is recommended for CI.
rationales: The observed connection came from the project file.
Managed servers rank above all other scopes.
Transport type doesn't change approval behaviour.

sources.title: MCP in Claude Code — Claude Code docs
Headless mode and CI — Claude Code docs

questions.stem: Platform engineering is publishing a new remote MCP server for Claude Code users. Which transport should they choose?
options: SSE
stdio over SSH
Streamable HTTP, with OAuth for authorization
A shared network drive the client polls
questions.explanation: For remote servers MCP uses Streamable HTTP, and Claude Code recommends the HTTP transport while marking SSE deprecated. OAuth is the recommended authorization approach for remote servers.
rationales: stdio is for local servers launched by the client.

sources.title: MCP in Claude Code — Claude Code docs
MCP architecture — MCP docs

questions.stem: Mid-tool-call, an MCP server needs the user to authorise access to their brokerage account through the broker's OAuth flow. How should it involve the user under the 2026-07-28 protocol?
options: Use elicitation in form mode to collect the user's brokerage password
Use sampling to have the model ask for the credentials
Use elicitation in URL mode to send the user to the broker's authorization page
Write the request into the tool result and hope the model relays it
questions.explanation: Elicitation's URL mode exists for credentials and OAuth flows, and form mode must not request secrets. Sampling is deprecated as of 2026-07-28 and would route secrets through the model.
rationales: Form mode must not request secrets.
Sampling is deprecated, and secrets shouldn't pass through the model.
Unreliable, and it places instructions inside tool results.

sources.title: MCP client concepts — MCP docs

questions.stem: A team wants a single API request to return a JSON object (validated by `output_config.format`) whose fields carry Citations-API citations into the source guidelines. What should the architect tell them?
options: It works as long as the schema sets `additionalProperties: false`
Ask for citations as a free-text field and trust them
Force the tool with `tool_choice` to combine them
Citations and structured outputs are incompatible in one request; return a cited answer and convert it to JSON in a separate step, or choose one feature
questions.explanation: The docs state that Citations and structured outputs are incompatible and return 400 together. A two-step design keeps the guaranteed-valid citations, while asking for citations as a free-text field loses that guarantee.
rationales: The schema setting doesn't remove the incompatibility.
Loses the guarantee that citations point to real locations.
Forced tool choice returns 400 on the newest models and doesn't enable citations.

sources.title: Citations — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A RAG design document says "embed chunks with the Anthropic embeddings endpoint". What correction should the architect make?
options: None; use the default Claude embedding model
Use Claude to generate embeddings through the Messages API
Anthropic doesn't offer its own embedding model; pick a third-party provider (the docs use Voyage AI as the example), evaluate alternatives, and set `input_type` for queries and documents
Skip embeddings and rely on BM25 alone for all queries

Ask for a longer, more detailed summary so nothing is omitted

Mean output length per task

questions.stem: An operations agent is about to go to pilot and has no evals. The team plans to spend two months writing 2,000 synthetic tasks first. What is the better starting point?

Use a public agent benchmark as the eval set
Have one senior engineer hand-grade 10 tasks per week
Start with about 20–50 tasks drawn from real failures and incidents, grade the outcomes, read transcripts, and grow the set over time
questions.explanation: Anthropic's agent-eval guidance is to start small with 20–50 tasks taken from real failures, rather than delaying for a large synthetic set. Grading outcomes and reading transcripts quickly shows where the agent actually breaks.
rationales: Complaints are a lagging and biased signal; you need a pre-release gate.
Public benchmarks don't reflect your tools, data or failure modes.
Too small and slow; favour more automated cases.
Correct. Small, real and outcome-graded, then grown.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.stem: A coding-agent eval fails a run whenever the agent's tool calls differ from a recorded 'golden' sequence. Reviewers find many failed runs produced correct, test-passing patches by a different route. How should grading change?
options: Grade the outcome, for example whether the repository's tests pass and the requested change is present, instead of the exact tool-call path
Keep the golden sequence and prompt the agent to follow it exactly
Replace all automated grading with human review
Reduce the agent's tools so only the golden path is possible
questions.explanation: Agents often find valid paths the eval author didn't foresee, so path-matching penalises correct work and measures the wrong thing. Grading the end state with code (tests pass, change present) is objective and reflects the real goal.
rationales: Over-constrains the agent and still measures conformity, not correctness.
Human review is slow and expensive; an objective code check exists here.
Hobbles the agent to fit a flawed metric.

Any model with free-form commentary and no score
No judge; use answer length as a proxy for helpfulness
questions.explanation: Anthropic advises evaluating with a different model from the one that generated the output, and constraining and validating the grader's output. Calibration against human labels shows how far the judge's scores can be trusted.
rationales: Free-form commentary cannot be aggregated or gated on.
Length is a poor proxy and rewards verbosity.

sources.title: Define success and build evals — Claude API docs

questions.stem: A new eval suite for multi-step incident remediation shows a 30% pass rate, while the existing suite for routine ticket triage holds at 99%. A manager wants to block releases because '30% is failing'. What is the right interpretation?
options: Both suites should be near 100%, so block the release
Delete the remediation suite because it is too hard
The remediation suite is a capability eval, which is expected to start low and track progress; the triage suite is a regression eval, and a drop there is what should gate releases
Average the two suites and gate on 64.5%
questions.explanation: Capability evals measure what the agent can't yet do reliably, so they start at a low pass rate and give a hill to climb. Regression evals should sit near 100%, and a fall there signals a breakage worth blocking on.

Rewrite the agent as a multi-agent system so subagents share the work
Enable fast mode
Switch immediately to the smallest model tier without running evals

questions.stem: How should a team share build commands, architecture notes and conventions with Claude Code across all engineers?
options: A concise, reviewed project CLAUDE.md committed to the repository
Paste them into every prompt
Email them weekly
Each engineer writes their own notes
questions.explanation: A project CLAUDE.md is loaded automatically at session start and versioned with the code, so changes are reviewed like any other file. Keep it concise so it stays effective. Pasting or emailing conventions is inconsistent and is not loaded by Claude Code.
rationales: Correct: shared, automatically loaded and reviewed.
Repetitive and error-prone; engineers will forget or drift.
Email is not loaded into Claude Code sessions.
Produces inconsistent behaviour across the team.

questions.stem: A CI job running Claude Code hangs indefinitely. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model is too small
It was started in interactive mode instead of headless mode (-p), so it waits for input
CLAUDE.md is too long
Too many MCP servers
questions.explanation: Without -p, Claude Code starts an interactive session that waits for terminal input that never arrives in CI. Headless mode processes the prompt, prints the result and exits with a status code, which is what a pipeline needs.
rationales: Model size does not make a process wait for input.
Correct: interactive mode blocks waiting for input.
A long CLAUDE.md costs tokens but does not cause an indefinite hang.
Many servers can slow startup but would not normally wait forever.

questions.stem: One team reports Claude Code ignores a permission they allowed in their project settings. Other teams are unaffected. What should be checked first?
options: Delete CLAUDE.md
Reinstall Claude Code
Whether a higher-precedence setting (e.g., managed settings deny rule) overrides the project allow rule
Switch models
questions.explanation: When only one team's setting seems ignored, the usual cause is precedence: a managed or other higher-scope deny is evaluated before any allow. Running /status shows which settings sources loaded. (Project allow rules also wait for workspace trust, a related check.) Reinstalling or switching models does not change settings resolution.
rationales: CLAUDE.md does not grant or revoke permissions.
Reinstalling leaves the same settings files in place.
Correct: deny is evaluated first and managed settings win.
The model does not control permission evaluation.

questions.stem: Which metrics best evaluate the success of a Claude Code rollout?
options: Lines of code generated
Number of tokens consumed
Number of sessions started
Cycle time, PR throughput, defect/rollback rates and cost per engineer
questions.explanation: A rollout should be judged on delivery outcomes and cost, not activity. Lines generated, tokens and sessions show usage, which can rise while quality falls. Pair outcome metrics with cost per engineer to judge value.
rationales: Volume is not value and can reward bloat.
Token use is a cost input, not an outcome.
Session counts measure activity, not impact.
Correct: outcome and cost metrics together.

questions.stem: How should approved MCP servers be distributed to engineering teams?
options: Commit approved servers to each repo's .mcp.json and use centrally managed MCP configuration for org-wide control
Hard-code server credentials in CLAUDE.md
Disable MCP entirely
Each developer finds and installs servers themselves
questions.explanation: A project .mcp.json shares vetted servers with everyone who clones the repo, and interactive sessions ask before using them. Managed MCP configuration outranks every other scope, giving admins central control. Credentials never belong in CLAUDE.md.
rationales: Correct: shared through the repo and governed centrally.
Leaks secrets into a committed, model-visible file.
Throws away the value of approved integrations.
Ungoverned; every engineer picks unvetted servers.

questions.stem: Platform engineering puts `"model"` set to a cost-efficient model in managed settings, yet usage reports show engineers still running a more expensive model. What change actually restricts which models engineers can use?
options: Repeat the model setting in every repository's .claude/settings.json
Add availableModels (or deniedModels) to managed settings
Add a line to the managed CLAUDE.md telling Claude which model to use
Ask engineers to set the model in their user settings
questions.explanation: A managed model value is only a default that users can change in-session. Restricting the selectable models requires availableModels or deniedModels in managed settings. Project settings rank below managed, and CLAUDE.md text cannot change model selection.
rationales: Still just a default, and at lower precedence than managed.
Correct: these keys restrict the selectable models.
CLAUDE.md is model-facing guidance; it cannot lock the harness's model choice.
User settings are the lowest scope and fully under user control.

questions.stem: A security team writes a pre-tool-use hook script that detects writes to `infra/prod/` and exits with status 1. In testing, the writes still happen and only a warning appears. What is the fix?
options: Move the rule into CLAUDE.md so the model sees it
Raise the hook timeout above the default
Make the hook exit with code 2 when it detects a violation
Convert the hook to run after the tool call instead
questions.explanation: Claude Code hooks block only on exit code 2; other non-zero codes are treated as non-blocking errors. The docs say a hook meant to enforce policy should use exit 2. Running after the tool call is too late to prevent the write.
rationales: The hook ran; timeout is not the issue.
Correct: exit 2 is the blocking signal.
A post-tool hook fires after the write already happened.

questions.stem: A nightly CI job runs `claude -p` to triage failing tests. Results vary between runners because some developers' hooks, plugins and MCP servers load from the build image. What is the best way to make runs reproducible?
options: Run with --bare and pass the needed context and tools explicitly
Switch the job to an interactive session driven by a terminal emulator
Delete CLAUDE.md from the repository
Add a CLAUDE.md note telling Claude to ignore plugins
questions.explanation: --bare skips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, so the run depends only on what the job passes in. The docs recommend it for CI. Deleting CLAUDE.md or adding notes does not stop other components loading.
rationales: Interactive sessions are the wrong tool for CI and add fragility.
Removes useful shared context and leaves hooks/plugins/MCP loading.
Guidance cannot stop the harness loading components.

questions.stem: A pipeline calls `claude -p --output-format json --json-schema schema.json` and writes `structured_output` to a release-notes file. Occasionally the file contains `undefined` and the job still passes. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Ask for the JSON inside a code fence and parse it with a regex
Retry the step unconditionally three times
Lower the model's effort level to make responses shorter
Fail the step when the exit code is non-zero or structured_output is absent, and log the error result
questions.explanation: structured_output is absent when the run failed, so the pipeline must check for it (and the exit code) rather than assume it exists. Gating on it turns silent bad output into a visible failure. Regex parsing and blind retries mask the problem.
rationales: Less reliable than the schema-backed field.
Hides failures and can still write bad output.
Correct: gate on exit status and field presence.

questions.stem: After a Claude Code upgrade, a headless CI job that used to run `npm test` now reports the Bash calls as denied, though nothing in the repo changed. What best explains this and fixes it?
options: The MCP servers failed to start; restart the runner
Headless -p now starts in Manual mode, so calls needing approval are denied; pre-approve the specific commands or set an explicit permission mode
The model refused the request; rewrite the prompt more forcefully
The project CLAUDE.md is too long; trim it
questions.explanation: In recent versions, -p starts in Manual mode, and any call that needs approval is denied because nobody can approve it. The fix is to allow the exact commands the job needs (or choose an appropriate --permission-mode) rather than broadly bypassing permissions. The other options do not produce permission denials.
rationales: MCP failures show up as server errors, not Bash denials.
Correct: explicit, scoped approvals for unattended runs.
This is a harness permission decision, not a model refusal.
Length affects context, not permission evaluation.

questions.stem: Engineers in one repo report that Claude Code seems to ignore part of their configuration. Which two steps should an enablement engineer take first? (Select two.)
options: Run /status to see which settings sources actually loaded
Reinstall Claude Code on every affected laptop
Run claude doctor to find settings entries that were rejected
Switch the team to a larger model
questions.explanation: /status shows the settings sources in effect and claude doctor lists rejected entries, which together explain most 'my config is ignored' reports. Reinstalling keeps the same settings files, and model choice does not affect configuration loading.
rationales: Costly and leaves the same configuration in place.
Correct: surfaces invalid or rejected entries.

questions.stem: Leadership wants an org-wide dashboard of Claude Code sessions, cost, commits and pull requests per team, without asking each engineer to configure anything. What should the platform team do?
options: Ask engineers to paste session summaries into a spreadsheet weekly
Commit OTEL exporter variables in each repo's .claude/settings.json
Enable Claude Code OpenTelemetry through the managed settings env and send metrics to the company's collector
Turn on logging of full user prompts so cost can be inferred
questions.explanation: Claude Code emits OpenTelemetry metrics such as session count, cost, commits and pull requests, and admins can turn it on centrally through managed settings env. Repository settings files cannot set the OTEL exporter variables. Logging full prompts is unnecessary for these metrics and adds privacy risk.
rationales: Repository settings cannot set the exporter variables.
Prompt content is redacted by default for privacy and isn't needed for cost.

questions.stem: A CI gate runs Claude Code headlessly with `--output-format stream-json`. The team wants the gate to fail fast when a required MCP server does not connect at startup, and to flag runs slowed or degraded by retried API calls. Which stream signals should it inspect? (Select two.)
options: The mcp_server_errors list in the system/init event
The model's self-reported confidence in its final message
system/api_retry events showing retried API calls
The number of lines in the generated review
questions.explanation: The system/init event lists mcp_server_errors (and plugin_errors), so a gate can fail fast when a required server is missing instead of producing weak output. system/api_retry events record retried API calls, which flags degraded runs. Self-reported confidence and output length are not reliable health signals.
rationales: Correct: fail the job when a required server errors at startup.
The model may not know a server is missing.
Correct: api_retry events show retried API calls, the signal for degraded runs.
Length says nothing about tool availability.
